title: A Name Made From the Content: How Version Control Knows Two Things Are the Same

questions.question: Two folders of a project need to be compared to see whether they are the same. What makes that cheap?
options: Giving every file a short name made from its content, so equal names mean equal content
questions.explanation: That is what a version control tool does with every file.

questions.question: What does one changed character do to a good hash?
options: Changes about half of the bits wherever the change is: a mean of 32.4 of 64, between 16 and 44, over every place in a 200 character text
questions.explanation: That spread is why equal names can be trusted to mean equal content.

questions.question: Why are a snapshot's file names combined with xor?
options: Xor gives the same answer in whatever order, and a folder has no order, so a name that depended on one would change when nothing did
questions.explanation: The same three files in two orders had the same snapshot name.

questions.question: A file is renamed and its content is unchanged. What happens to its names?
options: Its content name is the same and its name in the snapshot is different
questions.explanation: A content name does not depend on what the file is called.

questions.question: Two versions of a hundred files, one edited: how many different contents have to be stored?
options: 101: the ninety-nine unchanged files have the same name in both and are stored once
questions.explanation: That is why a commit is quick and small, even for a large project.

questions.question: Why is FNV-1a not enough for a tool that has to resist somebody trying to make two files collide?
options: It is not a cryptographic hash, and a 64 bit name could in a large enough store give two contents the same name
questions.explanation: The real tool uses a longer hash for that reason.
